items.title: Joanne Brackeen interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 10, 2001
items.q: She’s a good friend. She’s always calling.

ctx.x: I just had a swimming class yesterday. That was fun. Kind of cold for a while, I kind of did it.
Well you said you like to be near the water, so it keeps you healthy. I know you’ve done Marian McPartland’s show.

A couple of times. She’s a good friend. She’s always calling. She’s an amazing person. Always sending me articles, she does this with people, sends them articles on themselves that they never would have seen. She’s unbelievable, as well as getting better at the piano. I think she’s playing this week at the, it’s part of Lincoln Center, where they have duets. The Penthouse.

items.title: Marian McPartland interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, April 26, 1997
items.q: And I was in it and the Maria Schneider big band and Joanne Brackeen.

ctx.x: I suppose in a perfect world it might not be necessary to have — I was just reading the other day that I think in two weekends there will be a women’s jazz festival in Washington I think it is. So maybe, as I said in a perfect world it wouldn’t be necessary to have a “women’s” jazz festival, but they would just have a jazz festival there would be a proportional amount of women players.

Well we always said this, like when they had the Kansas City women’s festival, that was a long time ago, I think you were probably a real young boy then — I can’t remember how long ago, gee maybe it’s 15 or 20 years — and this was the, like the biggest jazz festival ever. Mary Lou Williams played it and I played it and Toshiko Akiyoshi had her big band, and I mean it was a large event. And they carried that on for three or four years and then they ran out of money. So actually, what Billy Taylor is doing, it’s…
It’s almost the same in sports you know. They’re trying so hard to have professional women’s basketball for instance and it’s an uphill battle I guess.

items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I don’t think of myself as having a proper apprenticeship, like for instance Barbara Carroll, and JoAnne Brackeen, who played with Stan Getz.

ctx.x: Yeah. How did . . . or very little . . . how do you, how does that, what is your take on that being as opposed to the way things were when you came to New York? What are the pros and cons?

As a matter of fact I don’t think of myself as having a proper apprenticeship, like for instance Barbara Carroll, and JoAnne Brackeen, who played with Stan Getz. I’ve never played with any groups except Jimmy’s, and in a way that was an apprenticeship for learning how to be in show biz and how to . . . But as far as learning tunes and getting into bebop and all the things I did do, I did that by myself, not through being with other groups. But I wish I had done that. The fact that they’re all doing this now. It’s…
Wynton. I guess Wynton’s larger than life. He has all kinds of help from every angle, and he’s . . . I don’t know.
